# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES) markedly reduced restenosis but left an enduring legacy. There remains a 2% to 3% per year incidence of stent-related events beyond 1 year following implantation regardless of stent type; this ongoing annual risk lasts at least 15 years, and its pathogenesis may relate to the common presence of a metallic frame, which distorts and constrains the vessel, limits vasomotion and adaptive vascular remodeling, and serves as a nidus for chronic inflammation, neoatherosclerosis, thrombosis, and strut fracture [1]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to provide transient mechanical support and drug delivery, then disappear, theoretically restoring vascular structure and function.

## Rationale and early proof of concept

The dominant first-generation device, the Absorb scaffold (Abbott Vascular), was constructed from a poly-L-lactic acid backbone with a poly-D,L-lactic acid coating eluting everolimus [2]. A fully bioabsorbable drug-eluting coronary stent that scaffolds the vessel wall when needed and then disappears once the acute recoil and constrictive remodelling processes have subsided has theoretical advantages; the device has a poly-L-lactic acid backbone providing support and a poly-D,L-lactic acid coating that controls release of everolimus [2]. The first-in-man ABSORB trial established feasibility [2], and at 2 years the stent was bioabsorbed, had vasomotion restored and restenosis prevented, and was clinically safe, although late luminal enlargement due to plaque reduction without vessel remodelling needed confirmation [3].

## Pivotal randomized trials

Several randomized trials compared Absorb BVS with cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents (EES). ABSORB II tested mechanistic endpoints, but at 3 years the trial did not meet its co-primary endpoints of superior vasomotor reactivity and non-inferior late luminal loss, and a higher rate of device-oriented composite endpoint due to target vessel myocardial infarction was observed in the Absorb group [4]. ABSORB China demonstrated angiographic non-inferiority: in this multicenter randomized trial, BVS was noninferior to CoCr-EES for the primary endpoint of in-segment late loss at 1 year [5]. The largest registration trial, ABSORB III, randomized 2,008 patients with coronary artery disease to BVS versus cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents and demonstrated noninferior rates of target lesion failure at 1 year [6].

The all-comers AIDA trial reflected routine practice. There was no significant difference between the two groups in the primary outcome of target-vessel failure; however, the bioresorbable scaffold was associated with a significantly higher incidence of overall and very late device thrombosis through 2 years of follow-up [7].

## The thrombosis signal and pooled evidence

A consistent excess of scaffold thrombosis emerged across studies. An early meta-analysis found that compared with everolimus-eluting metallic stents, bioresorbable scaffolds had similar rates of repeat revascularisation at 1 year despite inferior mid-term angiographic performance, but patients had an increased risk of subacute stent thrombosis [8]. A subsequent systematic review reported that the excess risk of BVS relative to EES for stent thrombosis through 2 years was significant (odds ratio 2.08; 95% CI 1.02–4.26) [9]. The seven-trial individual-patient-data analysis confirmed the trend [10], and pooled randomized data showed that BVS compared with EES resulted in higher 3-year rates of target lesion failure (11.7% versus 8.1%) driven by greater target vessel events [11]. A comprehensive network meta-analysis reinforced this: patients treated with the Absorb BVS had a significantly higher risk of definite or probable scaffold thrombosis than metallic DES, and the risk of very late scaffold thrombosis was highest with the Absorb BVS among comparators [12].

## Mechanisms, technique, and the resorption window

Thick struts, undersizing, and suboptimal deployment were implicated as drivers [13,14]. A multicenter analysis characterized clinical presentation, mechanisms, and predictors of scaffold thrombosis [15]. These insights motivated optimized implantation (predilatation, sizing, postdilatation). ABSORB IV enrolled an expanded population using improved technique; overall, 1296 patients were randomized to Absorb and 1308 to Xience, and the primary endpoint occurred in 7.8% of Absorb patients versus 6.4% of Xience patients, achieving non-inferiority [16]. Importantly, long-term ABSORB III data showed that cumulative 5-year adverse event rates were increased after BVS compared with everolimus-eluting stents, but the period of excess risk ended at 3 years, coincident with complete scaffold resorption [17]. The time-varying nature of risk was confirmed in pooled analyses [18,19,20].

## Acute coronary syndromes and complex lesions

BVS were also tested in higher-risk settings. The ISAR-Absorb MI trial compared everolimus-eluting BRS, which provide short-term scaffolding and drug delivery, versus durable-polymer EES in patients undergoing PCI for acute myocardial infarction in a non-inferiority design [21]. Registry and meta-analytic data in chronic total occlusions [22], bifurcations [23], and real-world cohorts [24] generally showed feasibility but recurrent safety concerns, prompting the FDA warning and the State of the Absorb expert consensus on patient and lesion selection and technique [25].

## Next-generation devices

Attention has shifted to thinner, stronger platforms. The higher scaffold thrombosis rates with first-generation BRS were likely due in part to insufficient radial strength necessitating larger strut profiles; current efforts focus on increasing tensile strength and reducing strut thickness [26]. Magnesium-based scaffolds are a leading approach: magnesium alloy has potential because it is a metal with high radial strength and less thrombogenic electrochemical properties than most implant metals [27]. The BIOSOLVE-II first-in-man study evaluated the DREAMS 2G (Magmaris) device [28], and the next-iteration DREAMS 3G (BIOMAG-I) reported encouraging one-year results [29]. In ST-elevation myocardial infarction, the MAGSTEMI trial compared a magnesium scaffold with a permanent sirolimus-eluting stent [30].

## Conclusions

First-generation Absorb BVS did not fulfil their early promise, with excess target-vessel myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis concentrated within the resorption window. The lessons—thinner struts, meticulous sizing and deployment, and appropriate case selection—are guiding a new generation of polymeric and magnesium-based scaffolds that may yet realize the original concept of transient vascular support.
